title: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to standardize parts to lower costs
titleZh: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to standardize parts to lower costs
author: zdw
relevanceReason: 命中 1 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda will begin standardizing some vehicle parts in an effort to lower production costs, according to a report by Automotive News. The automakers will start with equalized quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses.Discussions are starting with Japan’s domestic suppliers, though international suppliers will be looped in soon.Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News. The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, announced the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week.In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact.CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images|Getty ImagesThe first discussions of standardization are set to include Japan’s domestic automotive parts suppliers, though international suppliers will be brought into the fold in time. The first standardization efforts are set to go into place next year, according to the AN report.The push to simplify and lower costs comes as Japan’s seven automakers, including Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Suzuki, work to fend off the increasingly competitive list of Chinese automakers. The automakers are said to hope that they can channel the money saved by homogenizing into new innovations.“We all share this strong sense of crisis, creating a momentum for change,” Sato said. “Based upon our sense of a crisis, we decided to choose these three areas.”➡️ Skip the lot. Let Car and Driver help you find your next car.Jack Fitzgerald’s love for cars stems from his as yet unshakable addiction to Formula 1. After a brief stint as a detailer for a local dealership group in college, he knew he needed a more permanent way to drive all the new cars he couldn’t afford and decided to pursue a career in auto writing. By hounding his college professors at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, he was able to travel Wisconsin seeking out stories in the auto world before landing his dream job at Car and Driver. His new goal is to delay the inevitable demise of his 2010 Volkswagen Golf.

comments.textRawHtml:
Ford and GM have been doing this since 2002 with the GM–Ford 6-speed automatic transmission [0]. The companies worked together on the design and ultimately worked with Allison Transmission on its manufacture.

One key difference between each company's implementation had to do with the shifting solenoids and the electronics. But as far as I know the actual clutch pads and gearing were the same.

children.author: lelanthran
children.textRawHtml:
> Ford and GM have been doing this since 2002 with the GM–Ford 6-speed automatic transmission [0]

All the manufacturers have been doing it since even before that, with major items like engines and transmissions.

What they haven't been doing is standardising all those other parts that need replacing. For example, standardising on the wheel hub+knuckle for 15-inch, 16-inch, 17-inch and 18-inch wheels will let wheels of the specific size use the same disks, calipers, pads, balljoint, wheel bearing, CV joint and all the sensors (wheel speed, brake, etc).

I see no reason why two different SUVs on 17-inch wheels need completely different brake pads shapes, when both sets have the same surface area, require the same performance profile, etc, but that's what we have now.

You can do the same with almost every mechanical and electrical subsystem in a car, and still have a large variety in cars produced. After all, car manufacturers don't manufacture their own tyres and batteries, do they? They don't manufacture they own wheels.

Even the things that are specific to them, they outsource anyway - they don't each have their own windscreen manufacturer, they outsource that. The already outsource all the glass, all the oils and fluids, all the pipes, etc, it's jus that they produce incompatible designs so that the actual parts manufacturer has to charge a jig setup fee for each of them. Standardising on parts brings in economies of scale.

children.author: thelastgallon
children.textRawHtml:
> They’re a Right to Repair aligned business model.

We need right to repair (for many many good reasons), but this must be reframed and articulated to legacy car manufacturers as Commoditize your complement.

Legacy mfrs know (lets pretend) how to make cars, but they definitely don't know how to make batteries. It looks like we are headed towards a CATL and BYD duopoly. The first thing car manufacturers must do is standardize batteries and open source BMS and make batteries replaceable like batteries. There may not be current competition, but enable future competition. Eventually, some govts somewhere will start subsidizing locally sourced batteries, then your cars are future proofed and ready to swap in without changing design.

We can avoid the phone duopoly, if car manufacturers recognize their days are over, its all EVs, they still have some brand value (fwiw) and leverage that brand value with mostly commoditized components, pretty much everything except for the shell. These are batteries, all electrical components, heat pumps, sensors, electronics, etc. Make everything standardized just like wheels. And all manners of software should be open source: BMS, ADAS, self-driving, etc. And infotainment, instrument panel controls replacing carplay/android with a corresponding phone app (eventually evolving into a third phone ecosystem).

Legacy mfrs have learnt by now that they don't know how to make batteries. What Happened to America's Giant EV Battery Factories: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6Jq9MADu8bA

children.author: dzonga
children.textRawHtml:
my take legacy manufacturers from Japan slept on the job.

the world is going electric. but they had everything to capture what most of the world needs in Extended Range Electric Vehicles - which are more practical than pure EVs.

they know how to make small engines (Honda, Yamaha), they know how to make hybrid powertrains (toyota) - they just needed to put out decent batteries and electric motors and not waffle about.

they can still capture that market since Chinese EREVs are not yet that good - compared to their EVs.

children.author: mech998877
children.textRawHtml:
As a mechanical engineer this comment strikes me as too optimistic and borderline naive.

There are hundreds of reasons why different steering components have different shapes. By the time you are down to designing the steering knuckles and wheel hubs of cars, you are already working with vehicle weight, geometry constraints (which are a big deal), backward compatibility to simplify supply chain, material availability, outside suppliers, manufacturability, steering ratios, existing tooling, trying to minimize unsprung weight, servicability, whether the car uses a mcpherson strut or some other suspension setup, FWD vs AWD, etc, etc, etc.

It is almost an overconstrained problem to design these parts for a single vehicle. The combinatorial explosion of how many different ways there are to design the part is worse than you think it is.

children.author: ExoticPearTree
children.textRawHtml:
> I see no reason why two different SUVs on 17-inch wheels need completely different brake pads shapes, when both sets have the same surface area, require the same performance profile, etc, but that's what we have now.

Because an SUV that has 17" wheels can weigh two tons or three tons or more. It can do 120 mph maximum speed or it can go to 160 mph or more.

The math changes really fast when it comes to stopping that SUV down based on those two parameters alone. You can see why different calipers, how many, brake disk size, type (ventilated or not), different sized brake pads.

children.textRawHtml:
I don’t think this is true at all. Towing and payload vary heavily across models, which is the most direct need to technical performance.

Different models are also targeting different driving characteristics. Higher performance pads bite more which might be undesirable for smooth, luxury vehicles. While those same pads and rotors would be problematic while towing.

children.author: lbriner
children.textRawHtml:
Not sure you are disagreeing though. Having different brake pads within a standard range would be normal enough, we are talking more about the private of high-cost items like the brake caliper itself.

For top-end vehicles, sure, they might want slightly more braking or slightly lighter components and will invest in that but for most cars, I suspect that more parts could be standardised.

Actually, a lot of parts are already standardised including wing mirrors, electronics and smaller engine components so it is possible to do but sure, it's scary giving up your engine design time and trusting that you can use the same engine as a rival but still have a USP for your customers.

children.author: cucumber3732842
children.textRawHtml:
Brakes got big and dirverse because "muh handlig" and "muh moose test" (and "muh $500 replacement rim when you hit a curb) drive tire and rim size. Big rims add weight. So they make the brakes lighter by using a bigger diameter rotor and smaller/lighter caliper. The move from traditional spindles and/or press in bearings to bolt on unit bearings hasn't helped either since you're carrying around a few pounds of extra mounting flange.

A big honking cast iron caliper grabbing 12" rotor that mounts from the back of the hub (to reduce the hat diameter letting you have swept area right up to the wheel bolt circle) can really take some heat and the whole thing will package in a 16" rim. But it ain't gonna be light. I get that we're gonna have different "classes" of performance and you won't put that brake assembly on a new land rover even if it has comparable demands to the old van but there is a whole lot of room to consolidate here.

children.author: numpad0
children.textRawHtml:
They can like idk, use exact same capiler mounting brackets or mounting screws or pre-cut brake hoses or things like that for vans and trucks, then fit differently sized pads or even the whole calipers each.

That will eliminate like, technically different washers and nuts used for screws to mount the truck calipers that goes this way versus van calipers that comes through this here using slightly longer screws, and that kinds of things add up.

A lot of comment heree seem to be fixated on metal parts, but I think it's more about plastics and wires and electronics. If you could use a common harneess for compacts and sedans and trucks going forward and backward and across... saves a lot of inventory cost.

children.author: SoftTalker
children.textRawHtml: There already is some commonality within manufacturers. Ever look under the hood or dashboard and notice a connector on the wiring harness that's not connected to anything? That's because they used the same harness as another model that needs that connector. It's cheaper to design, produce, stock, and manage one harness even if there's extra wire and connectors that aren't used on every car. It probably doesn't happen across manufacturers though, but there are SAE standard connector types at least.

children.author: limagnolia
children.textRawHtml: It is always a trade off between standardizing and differentiating.  At some point, performance and technology converge, and it is no longer worth it to differentiate designs, thus you standardize.  I am no expert on what parts have reached that point, but there likely are a lot that have.

children.author: lbriner
children.textRawHtml:
This!

We had this when the Peugeot 107, Citroen C1 and Toyota Aygo were basically the same car. For the manufacturers, there was a significant cost saving but ultimately you relied on brand loyalty to sell whichever of them was not the cheapest model since they varied but a not insignificant amount.

Of course, the other area where most manufacturers make their money is after-sales "Service" although since many dealers, at least in the UK, are independent, the manufacturer can't easily control the profitability of these. My wife uses a Hyundai dealer who are really poorly run. Hard to book the car in, really inconvenient "leave it with us all day" etc. so not sure that is a great way to make money in the current model.
